item.title: Rethinking inner speech through linguistic active inference
item.description:
Why do we talk to ourselves in our minds? I have spent years puzzling over this deceptively simple question.

Most of us experience a silent voice in our heads – narrating a tricky moment, rehearsing a difficult conversation, or quietly walking ourselves through a plan. Nearly a century ago, the developmental psychologist Lev Vygotsky offered a compelling origin story. As children grow, spoken dialogue with caregivers turns inward and becomes a tool for self-regulation and planning. That account tells us where inner speech comes from, yet a deeper puzzle remains. Why does the brain reach for language – a system built for talking to other people – when thinking alone?

Look closely at the research and contradictions pile up quickly. Talking to yourself helps on some tasks and makes little difference on others. Sometimes inner speech arrives effortlessly as a single clipped word, while at other times it unfolds as a deliberate back-and-forth debate. Some people describe an almost constant inner conversation, while others report little or no inner voice at all.

In my paper in Psychological Review, I propose a unifying framework called Linguistic Active Inference Theory (LAIT). At its heart is a simple idea. Inner speech is an internal action that helps the mind and body navigate uncertainty.

How silent words guide mind and body

Every waking moment, your brain tries to make sense of what your senses are taking in and decide what your body should do next. Living organisms stay on track by predicting incoming sights, sounds, and physical outcomes, then updating those expectations whenever reality surprises them – a process known as active inference.

When the world is familiar and predictable, perception and movement run smoothly on their own. When a situation becomes ambiguous or a decision is unclear, however, the mind needs a way to organise messy sensory detail and weigh possibilities beyond what is immediately in front of us. That is where inner speech comes in.

Language is compact, flexible, and generative. Putting an uncertain experience into words condenses sprawling sensory information into a sharp category your mind can work with, and putting an abstract goal into words unpacks it into concrete bodily steps. Crucially, what you say to yourself – and how you word it – alters both what you expect to perceive or do next and how firmly you hold onto that expectation.

Why your inner voice changes shape

Think about a moment just before leaving the house. You reach into your usual pocket and your keys are missing. One quiet word names what is absent – “Keys.” A confident sentence narrows down where to look – “If they aren’t here, they must be in my coat pocket” – and guides your hand straight to the coat. Even if your fingers touch a glove first, that confident wording keeps you searching that pocket a second time. When the pocket turns out empty, your inner speech shifts again into a brief internal exchange weighing options – “Maybe on the table? Or by the door?” The moment you spot the keys, the voice stops.

Seen through linguistic active inference, the changing shape of inner speech follows the structure of the uncertainty you face. Single words help pin down what something is, full sentences map out if-then steps for action, and internal dialogues weigh competing choices. When uncertainty is high and a problem can be captured in words, inner speech expands and coordinates with your eyes, posture, attention, and bodily arousal. When things become clear and routine, it condenses and fades into the background.

One framework across everyday thought, diversity, and distress

Framing inner speech as uncertainty-driven linguistic inference connects observations that used to sit in separate silos.

  • Why benefits are selective. Inner speech helps most when a task involves resolvable uncertainty that words can capture, and adds little when sensory cues are already clear or hard to put into words. Confident wording sharpens perception and action when expectations are right, and can entrench mistakes when expectations are wrong.
  • Why people differ so widely. People differ in how readily they reach for words when uncertain and how heavily they weight verbal expectations alongside visual imagery, bodily cues, and direct sensory evidence. A mind with little inner speech can still navigate the world effectively through non-verbal inference.
  • When inner speech turns unhelpful. The same mechanism also offers a fresh lens on mental health. When uncertainty feels impossible to resolve, inner speech can lock into repetitive negative loops (rumination). When internal verbal expectations are weighted too strongly relative to sensory input, internal speech may even be experienced as an external voice.

Looking ahead

A theory is only as useful as the predictions it lets us test – and potentially disprove. In the LISN Lab, we are putting linguistic active inference to the test by combining behavioural experiments, eye tracking, brain recordings (EEG), ultrasound imaging of tongue movements, physiological signals, and self-talking computational models. Together, these methods let us watch how silent language, brain activity, and bodily action coordinate in real time as uncertainty rises and falls.

Read the full paper in Psychological Review, explore our inner speech research, or try our 3-minute inner-voice self-test to see how your experience compares with more than a thousand adults.

Do you notice your inner voice shifting – or going quiet – as situations become clearer or more uncertain?
